en: Cannot shake the world and take revenge,
Cannot overthrow the chief and spill his blood,
Cannot fight and take lives,
Cannot thrust his spear and break their ranks—
The mighty Toltoi and Chynkojo
We destroyed in carnage.
When we met them in battle
And slew their heroes,
The warrior most skilled with the spear died,
And the mightiest man in all the world died.
Many khans who came were slain,
And everyone we encountered died.
Over branching passes and high slopes
That was the road we used to travel;
Those whom we fought, your uncle
Swept away with his army.
While the great warrior lived,
Your lionhearted uncle was a hero,
A lion and gray wolf of a champion
Who made the whole world submit.
The one who crushed all challengers—
Alas, that Choro was I.
My fortune failed, my strength departed,
The panther, the gray-wolf hero, was gone;
My days passed in servitude,
And now, my son, brave Seytek,
I stand before you ruined thus.
While the panther lived,
I carved up whole fat-tailed sheep to eat.
I used to wonder where hell,
The greatest misery and disaster, could be.
While my magnanimous lord lived,
I knew the world and filled it with uproar;
When I lost my generous lord,
I suffered torment and withered away.
When I rode to battle, I lacked nothing,
And carved up fat-tailed sheep to eat;
While my mighty uncle lived,
I used to say I would wreak slaughter
Not only among the Kyrgyz, but across the world.
There is no strength left in the waist I gird,
My heroic, generous champion is gone;
What lives today is gone tomorrow.
One day all will be crushed—
Yet you lie there voicing your regrets.
When you took aim
At an enemy who defied you,
Compelling the whole world to submit,
When you held dominion over it,
Breaking through dead ends and opening roads,
Striking everyone you met,
When you held dominion over all,
When you wore armor
No bullet could pierce to your flesh,
When you raided Kara-Shaar, Kambyl, and Beijing,
Striking those cities,
When you wore a sable cap
Trimmed with blue-black otter,
When you made the whole world submit
And fell upon it,
When you kneaded the whole world
As though it were dough,
When you scorched this mortal world
As though it were a fly,
When you broke through countless armies with your spear
And drove them round,
When you laid the world waste
And knew it as your own,
Mounting a charger and taking up your spear,
With a naked sword belted at your side,
Circling the city of the Khakan,
Which even winged flight could not reach,
When you held it under siege,
When you scourged
The Kaldai and the Shibe,
What were your power and strength,
Your prowess when entering combat?
What skill did you possess?
Has all your vigor failed?
While your uncle and companion lived,
What strength was yours?
Test your might;
Learn the measure of your strength.
If your ancient power remains,
Unless fate strikes us down with bullets,
How could we stay alive and do nothing?
Unless we face the black-hearted Kyyaz
And fight him,
Grappling until we spill his blood,
Struggling until we take his life,
May I die rather than live
If I do not raise open war;
May I sink away unborn.
The hero Kyyaz has grown eager—
I shall meet him in mortal combat!
The sly Kyyaz seems to have gone mad;
I shall wage a mighty war,
Attack with all my resolve,
And chase him as far as Beijing.
I shall slaughter every khan,
Rip open their ribs,
And pour their blood into wineskins!
If I do not wage a vast battle,
If this year I do not avenge
My father who passed into the next world,
If in Jeti-Özön I do not make the Jediger
Keep Jeti-Özön as their land,
And form the Jediger into a nation,
If I do not burn their slopes to embers
And destroy their Khan Kyyaz,
If I do not divert the river’s waters,
If I do not make the black-hearted Jediger
Seem like a fire gone cold,
If I do not crush their champions,
Slay all who oppose me,
And soothe my vengeful heart,
May I sink away unborn.
My sworn enemy is Khan Kyyaz;
I shall try my strength against him.
The one I will grapple with is Kanchoro—
Here is my true enemy!
My khan and uncle who cared for me,
You are a father in my father’s place;
Having lost the noblest one,
We used to set up ninety mattocks,
And test our strength with thunderous force,
Plunging into the tumult to seize them;
We would enter contests
Of endless, thrilling uproar.
While your great champion lived,
We reveled in games to our hearts’ content;
Birch trees growing on the open plain
We tore up by the roots.
We used to play kökbörü with a camel;
While the princely gray wolf lived,
Whenever roused, we went to war
And tested our strength.
The mountain ibex of Daңduu-Bash,
The cliff goat with its thick hide,
We would put into the tanning vat.
Before my fortunate mother,
Standing sole to sole and pulling,
We tore them apart piece by piece;
Our muscles were each as large as a fist—
Such was our former strength.
We held feasts and revelries,
Drinking kumis and courting girls,
Playing orompoi and winning prizes;
Such boundless games we played.
In the safe days of happiness,
While the joyous gray wolf lived,
When the multitude camped in delight,
Their cares forgotten,
With pleasure by day and games by night,
In those flourishing times,
When we had drunk our fill of kumis,
Red-dressed and slender-waisted,
The most graceful beauties—
When yesterday the girls and young wives watched us,
If bored, we went hunting roe deer;
Through ninety mattocks in a row
We shot our arrows,
And plunged into such delights.
When your vigor is still sound,
Then enter battle;
If your strength is whole,
Then fall upon the enemy,
And learn the measure of your prowess.
Take only what your power permits,
And exert your warrior’s strength.
Now put your vigor and might
Fully to the test.
Show courage and test your strength;
Test every bit of your former might.
Then Külchoro said:
“While the hero still lived,
When all my strength was at its height,
When I scorched sand and set stone aflame,
In the days when I raged,
Destroying lives and spilling blood,
In the days when I thirsted for battle,
When I grasped my sword and took up my spear,
And laid the enemy low,
Subduing all who faced me
And driving them before me,
When I sharpened
My red, Zulfiqar-like sword,
And crushed the hostile foe,
Chewing them to pieces,
When I spread tumult wherever I went
And threw all who resisted into panic,
When I wore armor
No flame could pierce to my flesh,
When I subdued the foes who shot at me
And drove them round—
Your uncle was strong as a lion;
Your poor uncle Choro
Had every power needed for combat.
While my lionhearted uncle lived,
We brandished battle-axes
And stood testing our strength;
When would we ever strike from afar?
Taking matchlock and bow in hand,
We tested our strength side by side,
And singled out our foes without relent.
While my panther uncle lived,
We were guardians of the people;
We bore the aspect of princes,
We were the black eyes of the spring,
We were panther-hearted heroes ourselves.
While the precious gray wolf lived,
We were red-flaming caps of steel,
A blazing crimson fire
That stirred strife wherever war cries rang.
While the panther lived,
We were dark, keen caps of steel,
The splendor of the foe when put to flight,
A darkly burning fire
No sudden assault could extinguish.
While my great warrior lived,
We were the wind in the narrow mountain pass.
Yielding to none who fought us,
We were champions, ravenous lions;
We were the gray wolf’s true eyes,
The very flower of heroes.
He broke through dead ends and opened roads,
And attacked whatever foe he met.
Konurbai came from the Khakan’s realm
To the lands along Ala-Too,
But while my warrior still lived,
He could not defeat him in combat.
Khans and Manchu lords were crushed;
When the seer in Beijing beheld my bearing,
He wept, saying, “He is no mere mortal.”
Thus the diviner in Beijing wept.
The great Kaldai rode out to war,
And Konurbai too was crushed;
Unable to endure my warrior,
The people of the Khakan wept.
When they diverted the flowing water
And left the Muslim people thirsty,
When the black Manchu and the countless Shibe
Were pressed hard by their Kaldai,
I crossed straight over and opened a road.
While my ruined uncle lived,
He never failed to raise laughter,
Yet burned to enter battle
And put his power and strength to the test.
My lion uncle was a champion;
Another mortal like my uncle
Will never again be fashioned
And given life in this world.
My towering uncle was a mighty hero—
Alas, this treacherous world!
No such warrior will arise from humankind.
His fortune was perfectly balanced;
